title: False Negative
body:
Predicted negative, actually positive. A miss: the model fails to flag something that is there.

**This is a Type II error**, rate $\beta$, and [[Type I and Type II Errors]] in [[STATISTICS]]
(MATH 2234) owns the full translation. Missing the wolf that is there.

It sits in the denominator of [[Sensitivity]], $\text{TP}/(\text{TP}+\text{FN})$, which is the
metric that exists to measure it. Note that precision does not involve this cell at all, so a model
can have excellent precision while missing almost everything, simply by only predicting positive
when it is certain.

Unlike $\alpha$, which you choose, $\beta$ depends on how large the effect you are trying to catch
is. A small signal is missed more often, so "how many do we miss" has no single answer until you
say how faint a case counts.

Which of this and [[False Positive]] is worse is a domain question, never a statistical one: a
screening test tolerates false alarms to keep this cell near zero, because a missed cancer costs
more than an unnecessary follow-up.

See [[Confusion Matrix]] for the four cells together.
